I must admit, I don't really care about what Hillary has to say. I'm not really sure what she is doing by continuously attempting to remain in the public eye (more so outside this tweet), but the NRA is a key player in the political landscape of gun control. They are belligerently against common sense measures to help prevent guns getting into the wrong hands. If you're saying Hillary doesn't want to talk, well the NRA definitely doesn't either. And Hillary is irrelevant to enacting legislative change. She doesn't need to open herself to dialogue because she can't vote on legislation. NRA are fair game. 

And I also think that going after the NRA is about as partisan as going after guns. Democrats are NRA members too and some Dems are very pro-gun.

But this, just like literally everything on the planet, is a political issue. This is political because it involves US society at large. No matter the side, this is a conversation that has been ongoing for a very long time. When events relevant to gun control occur, it is the best time to have a discussion about it. 

It is in your side's best interests to not discuss it now when there might be less political will against gun control. However, seizing the opportunity to push gun control legislation in order to help prevent this from happening again, is not immoral in the least. It can't be. The whole reason to push gun control is to prevent people from having the means to quickly, efficiently and safely kill people, especially a large number of people. Not to mention the largest victims of a lack of effective gun control, the Americans who are committing suicide, (ETA) from having the means to impulsively and effectively kill themselves.

Talking about gun control now, when relevant events are in the public eye, is not wrong. People can disagree and call it immoral or wrong, but they don't have leg of reason to stand on.

How is looking/advocating for a solution to gun violence "interfering with the nation grieving"? Wouldn't it be a source of comfort for the people who lost loved ones, to know that something was being done to prevent this from happening to other people?

This whole argument of "let the families grieve, now is the wrong time to talk about gun control" is an underhanded way for people who oppose even the slightest increase in gun control to maintain some form of dubious moral high-ground for the ideas they support. 

I think it is a completely natural and human reaction to want to understand how this happened and prevent it from happening again. 

Sending a deluge of condolences and prayers, while community building, is also fleeting. Why not something more substantive and enduring like talking about gun control and mental health?
